description_full: Aecon Group Inc., together with its subsidiaries, provide construction and infrastructure development services to private and public sector clients in Canada, the United States, and internationally. It operates through two segments, Construction and Concessions. The Construction segment focuses on civil infrastructure, urban transportation solutions, nuclear power infrastructure, utility infrastructure, and industrial infrastructure market sectors. The Concessions segment engages in the development, financing, building, and operation of construction projects by way of public-private partnership contract structures. This segment also provides development of domestic international public-private partnership; private finance solution; developing strategic partnerships; leading and/or participating in development teams; and operations and maintenance of infrastructure assets services. Aecon Group Inc. was formerly known as Prefac Concrete Co. Ltd. and changed its name to Aecon Group Inc. in June 2001. The company was founded in 1867 and is headquartered in Toronto, Canada.

financial_summary: Aecon Group Inc. is a mid-cap industrials business with a $2.7B market cap on $3.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 2% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 6% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $41M in free cash flow — roughly 1 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 8.35× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 1.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 1.5%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
